(c) Yes Sir. There are several reasons for under-utilisation of budget 
provisions. Some of these are (i) incomplete proposals received, (ii) requisite 
documents not enclosed, (iii) inspection reports and recommendations not 
received, (iv) Withholding of grants due to complaints received against the 
organizations and (v) clarification sought from  the organizations etc.  to 
name  a  few. 
2 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
However in 1999-2000, more than 90% of the budgeted amount was utilized. 
(d) In order to ensure optimal utilization of the budgetary provisions, the 
Ministry has initiated a number of steps. The State Governments have been 
asked to sponsor cases especially in those areas where budgetary allocations 
have remained under-utilised. The Minist ry has been requesting NGOs with 
good track record to come forth with proposals for extension of their services 
to un-served areas with financial support from the Government. This Ministry 
has also publicized its schemes thro ugh the issue of a compendium and a 
module on Grant-in-aid assistance to voluntary organizations was recently 
included in the Ministry's website. These contain useful information 
pertaining to the various Schemes of the Ministry. 
SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: Sir, the Minister has said that in the 
year 1999-2000, more than 90 per cent of the budgeted amount was utilised. I 
would like to know from the Minister the actual provision made in the year 
1998-99, 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 and the actual am ount sanctioned and 
disbursed during these years. 
The Minister has also mentioned five reasons for the under-utilisation of 
the budgeted provisions. So, is her Ministry planning to have any orientation 
programme to give orientation to the voluntary organisations, NGOs, in the 
respective States so that whenever applications are received, they are 
complete in every respect so that the question of under-utilisation of 
budgeted provisions does not arise? 
SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI: Sir, the actual figures that the hon. 
Member asked are: In 1998-99, it was Rs. 119.57 crores; in 1999-2000, it 
was Rs. 180.82 crores; and now, it is Rs. 170.42 crores. 
Regarding the orientation programme, we do not have a specific orientation 
programme to teach people how to fill the forms. However, we have not only 
made the forms much easier but also pu t a website that they can access. If 
they come here, we help them. If they do not, they write to us their queries, if 
they have doubts. More people are applying today than have ever done 
earlier. I do not think that we need an  orienation programme to teach how to 
fill the forms.

Standard procedure to value to assets of PSUs 
1622. SHRI R. MARGABANDU : Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
 what is the standard procedure adopted by the Disinvestment 
Commission to value the assets of the PSU; 
 whether there is any proposal to constitute a joint Parliamentary 
Committee to value to assets of the PSUs which are going to be disinvested; and 
 if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The Disinvestment 
Commission has examined the issue of valuation of equityvaluation of assets in 
their report of December, 1996 on "Disinvestment • Strategy and Issues" and 
observed as under:— 
Valuation 
The valuation of equity of a firm gains importance in case of disinvestment 
of companies which are not listed or in cases where capital markets may not 
fully reflect the intrinsic worth of a share 
59 

RAJYA SABHA        [12 MARCH, 2001] 
disinvested earlier. Valuation should be independent, transparent and free from 
bias. 
Valuation Methods 
There are three basic approaches: The discounted cash-flow relates the value of 
an asset to the present valu e of expected future cash flows on the asset. In the 
second method, relative valuation is used to estimate the value of an asset by 
looking at the pricing of comparable assets relative to a common variable like 
earnings, cash flows, book value or sales. In the third method, the net asset value 
of the share is used as a basis for valuation." 
Dealing with the issues regarding valuation methods and their application the 
Commission inter-alia stated that 
"It is true that valuation does make use of quantitative models but the inputs 
leave plenty of room for subjective judgements. At the same time there may 
be no such thing as a precise estimate of a value. Even after the end of the 
most careful and detailed valuation of a company, there could be uncertainty 
about the final numbers as they are shaped by assumptions about the future of the 
company and of the company." 
The Disinvestment Commission further observed in its 1st report as follows: 
"Where Government continues to hold 51% or more of the share 
holding, the valuation will relate mainly to the shares of the companies 
and not to the assets of the company. On the other hand, where shares are 
sold through strategic sale and management is transferred to the strategic 
partner, the valuation of the enterprise would be different as the strategic 
partner will have control of the management. In such cases, the valuation of 
land and other physical assets should also be computed at current market values 
in order to fix the reserve price for the strategic sale." 
 No, Sir. 
 Valuation of physical assets, wherever considered necessary, is done by 
professional valuers.

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITELY): (a) to (e) A Statement containing the gist of the 
recommendations of the Committee on State Funding of Elections (Indrajit 
Gupta Committee) is laid on the Table of the House (See below). In this 
connection it may be stated that the comments/views of the State 
Governments/Union territory Administrations and different concerned 
Ministries/ Departments in the Central Government and the Election 
Commission of India on these recommendations has been solicited and many 
of them have not so far given their response in this regard. On receipt of their 
comments/views, these may be discussed with the political parties as part of 
the process of reform of electoral laws at an appropriate time. The reform of 
electoral laws is, however, a continuous and ongoing process and can be 
carried out only through consensus among political parties, which is a time 
consuming process and, therefore, no time frame for taking a decision/action 
thereon can be suggested in this regard. Government, however, intends to 
continue interaction with the political parties in this regard. 
Statement 
Gist   of recommendations   of committee  on  state funding   of elections 
(Indrajit Gupta Committee) 
1. State Funding of Elections: The Committee has recommended, to being 
with, only partial State assistance, in Kind only in the form of certain 
facilities, to recognized political parties in a way that it provides them relief 
not only in carrying out their electoral activities and meeting partly the cost of 
essential items of electioneering campaigns of their candidates, but also helps 
them partially in the current adminstration of their day to day functioning 
during non-election period. Gradually, mo re and more of their expenses' 
burden can be progressively shifted to the State so that ultimately all of their 
legitimate expenses become a charge on the State. In this respect, the 
Committee has recommended creation of a separate Election Fund to which 
the Central Government may contribute at the rate of Rs. 10/pct elector i.e. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
about Rs. 600/- crores annually. The State Governments also, all taken 
together, may contribute proportionately Rs. 600/- crores annually to the 
Fund. 
In its report, the Committee has also speci fied the nature of facilities to be 
provided to the recognized political parties and their candidates at State cost. 
These include:— 
(I) For recognized political parties: 
(i) Suitable rent-free accommodation for its headquarter. 
(ii) One rent-free telephone, with STD facility with a specified number of 
telephone calls over and above the free calls permitted to any 
subscriber. 
(iii) Sufficient free air time on the State owned media; certain additional 
time on the basis of votes polled; permission to use the allotted time 
for their propaganda in the manner they like and not necessarily for 
speeches alone. 
( i v )    R e g u l a t i o n    o f    p r i v a t e    c h a n n e l s    f o r    f a i r    a n d    b a l a n c e d  
presentation of the views of all parties. 
(II) For Candidates of recognized Parties: 
(i) Specified quantity of petrol/diesel. 
(ii) Specified quantity of paper for printing. 
(iii) Postal stamps of a certain specified amount. 
(iv) Five copies of electoral rolls in addition to the copies of the rolls 
presently being provided as per rules. 
(v) For an assembly election, one set of loudspeakers and for a 
parliamentary election, one set of loudspeakers for every assembly 
segment, subject to a maximum of sit such sets. 
(vi) For an assembly election, one te lephone with a speci fied number of 
free calls, and for a parliamentary election, at the rate of one 
telephone for every assembly segment, subject to a maximum of six 
telephones. 
(vii) On the day of poll, some minimum arrangements may be made for 
the candidates' camps at each polling station. 
106 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) Supply of refreshments and food packets to the counting agents 
inside the counting hall. 
2. Maintenance of Accounts by Political Parties and Audit thereof: 
(i) Political parties should compulsorily submit their annual accounts 
regularly to the Income Tax Authorities showing all details of their 
receipts and expenditure. 
(ii) No political party which has failed to submit its annual return for the 
previous assessment year under the Income Tax Act should be eligible 
for any State funding. 
(iii) The Chartered Accountant may be selected by the political party itself. 
The Income Tax authorities will, however, be tree to have a further 
check by their own agencies of returns submitted by parties. 
(iv) Each party receiving State subsidy should also file a complete account of its 
election expenditure during an election of the Election Commission in 
the format prescribed by the Commission. 
(v) All subscriptions, donations received by a party above the amount of Rs. 
10,000/-should be by means of a cheque/bank draft and should be 
mentioned in party accounts. 
3. Ban on donation by Companies to political parties: 
The question whether there should be any ban on donations by companies and 
corporate bodies for political purposes may be decided by the Government 
and Parliament in their collective wisdom. Ban on donations by Government 
Companies for political purposes should continue. 
4. Inclusion of expenses of political parties in the Election expenses 
of candidates for the purpose of ceiling on Election expenses: 
The question whether election expenses of political parties and other bodies 
or associations and individuals should be included or not in the accounts of 
election expenses of candidates may be decided by the Government/Parliament in 
their collective wisdom. However, apparent  contradiction  between  the  
provisions  of Section  77(1), 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
Explanation 1 of Representation of the People Act, 1951 and Section 171H of 
Indian Penal Code needs to be resolved as the former permits political 
parties and all other bodies or associations or individuals to make election 
expenses for any candidate without his authorization whereas the latter 
prohibits it. 
5. Empowering of the Election Commission of India to fix ceiling on Election 
expenses before every general election. 
Periodic revision of election expenses may continue to be done by the 
Central Govemment in consultation with the Election Commissiton of India 
as at present.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL

the Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 has been replaced by a new Act called the 
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 to bring the

 the provisions of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of

RAJYA SABHA        [12 MARCH, 2001] 
Children) Act, 2000 shall come into force with effect from the 1st day of 
April, 2001. 
Statement 
The salient features of the Juvenile Justice (care and protection of children) 
ACT, 2000 
 It prescribes a uniform age of 18 year s for both the boys and girls to be 
treated as children. 
 The Act also directs that the cases related to juveniles should be completed 
within a period of four months. 
 It has also been made compulsory to set up Juvenile Justice Board 
(previously known as Juvenile Court) and Child Welfare Committee 
(previously known as Juvenile Welfare Board) either for a District or a 
group of Districts. Previously if there was no Juvenile Court or Juvenile 
Welfare Board in existence then the powers of these Courts and Boards 
could be exercised by DM/ SDM/Me tropolitan Magistrate or Judicial 
Magistrate First Class. 
 All the offences against a juvenile have now been made cognizable 
offences. 
 It proposes to set up Special Juvenile Police Units through sensitization 
and training of such police personnel to perform their functions more 
effectively. 
 Role of voluntary organizations and local authorities has been specified 
for involving them at various stag es for handling and rehabilitating 
children. 
 The special emphasis has been given for rehabilitation and social 
reintegration of the children and the alternatives provided for the same

Subject: Unauthorised Encroachment and Illegal Constructions in Delhi. 
Sir, 
I am directed to say that the menace of illegal encroachment/ unauthorised 
construction in Delhi has been considered by the Government of India at its 
highest level and it has been decided to  eliminate this me nace with a firm 
hand. You are therefore, requested to take strong and prompt action against all 
illegal constructions/ unauthorised encroachments and also against misuses of 
land in violation of the provisions of the Master Plan of Delhi. The following 
measures are particularly required to be enforced strictly: 
(i) All illegal constructions should be demolished, not cosmetically but in 
toto. 
(ii) The cost of demolition should be recovered from the illegal builders 
within 15 days of demolition. In case of non-payment within 15 days, 
the amount due should be recovered as arrears of land revenue. 
(iii) In all cases of ille gal constructions, prosecution should invariably be 
launched against builders under the Delhi Municipal Corporation 
Act, Delhi Development Authority Act, New Delhi Municipal 
Council Act, etc. and the cases followed vigorously with the police 
authorities/courts. 
(iv) Wherever the property is on lease, action should be taken under the 
terms and conditions of lease agreem ent and re-entry effected within 
the shortest permissible period unde r such lease agreement. After re-
entry, physical possession of the property should be taken by 
invoking the provisions of P ublic Premises Eviction Act and 
damages collected immediately. The rates of damages/misuse 
charges should be the same as per the formula followed by the L & 
DO and approved by the Ministry of Urban Development. 
(v) In case of DDA flats, where cons tructions have come up beyond the 
condonable limits, cancellation of allotment should be carried out in 
addition to the demolition of the additional 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
construction.   Orders   in   respect   of   condonable   and   non-
condonable items are being issued separately. 
(vi) In cases, whereafter demoliti on reconstruction is done, personal 
responsibility of the officer incharge should be fixed and 
departmental action taken against him. 
(vii) In cases where illegal construction have taken placed on rural-
agricultural lands, action under the Provisions of the Delhi land 
Reforms Act, 1954, should also be taken and such lands should be 
taken over as per provisions of the Delhi Land Reforms Act. Action 
in this respect should be taken as soon as the plots are cut by the 
colon sers and construction done in the shape of boundary walls etc. 
In other words construction should be nipped in the bud. If it comes 
up, it should be demolished immediately. Action in this respect 
should also be taken by the concerned local agencies/DDA as per 
the bye-laws partaining to lay out/service plans, etc. 
(viii) In all cases where party obtains stay/status quo orders, prompt action 
to get the stay order vacated sh ould be taken an d higher court 
moved, wherever necessary. 
(ix) All Senior Field Officers should be asked to carry out physical 
inspection of the area under their charge and the Supervising Officer 
should also make surprise checks to  ensure that the subordinate staff 
takes immediate action to check/demolish unauthorised construction. 
Deterrent action should also be ta ken against the subordinate staff 
such as building Inspectors, Junior Engineers, Assistant Engineers, 
etc. who do not take prompt action. 
(x) Field Officers should be asked to maintain field diaries and submit 
them to the Supervisory Officer regularly. 
2. It is also requested that a monthly report should be sent to the Ministry 
of Urban Development by the 5th of each succeeding month.

*201. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether Govemment are aware that forest land in various parts of the 
country is under encroachment by mafias; 
 if so, whether the Forest Conservators have failed to protect the forest 
land and are in connivance with mafias in encroaching the same;

 whether Government have asked for detailed reports from State 
Governments about the area of forest la nd encroached by mafias; if so, the 
details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) Incidences of encroachments on forest land in various 
Slates/UTs have been occurring from time to time. The powers to take 
action against such encroachcrs vest s with the State Governments under 
Section 26 (reserve forests/proposed reserve forests/village forests) and 
Section 33 (in respect of protected forests) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and 
other relevant State Acts and Rules for the time being in force. The eviction 
of the encroachment is the responsibility of the State Governments who arc

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
also duty bound to intimate the areas en cioached to the Indian Council of 
Forest Research &. Education (ICFRE) for compiling the said information at 
the national level in the Forestry Statistics. As per the Forest Statistics Report 
published by the ICFRE in the year 200 0, an area of 7,14,855 hec. (Seven 
lakhs, fourteen thousand, eight hundred and fifty five hectares) of forcstlands 
were under encroachment in different States as on 1998. This information 
relates to only 19 States. The information for 1998 in relation to Arunachal 
Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Nagaland, 
Punjab, Sikkim, West Bengal, Lakshadweep and Pondicherry could not be 
compiled as these States have so far not submitted any information on the 
encroachments of forest lands. 
Encroachments are generally done by the local people for cultivation and 
construction of houses and normally take place because of laxity at local and 
field level. Absence of proper demarcation of forest boundaries on the 
ground and discrepancies in land records further compound the problem. 
Lack of resources and large number of vacancies affect the capacity of field 
formations to prevent encroachments and take effective eviction measures. 
At the recent meeting of State Mini sters of Environment & Forests at 
Coimbatore on 29th-30th January 2001, it was unanimously resolved to 
strengthen the infrastructure for conservation and protection of forests. These 
include filling up of the vacant posts of Forests Guards, Foresters, Range 
Forest Officers and Assistant Conservators of Forests on priority, lifting ban 
on recruitment of forestry personnel an d treating forestry appointments on 
similar lines to Police Department, infra structure such as roads, buildings, 
wireless equipment, vehicles, arms etc. required for forest protection shall be 
strengthened on priority, working plans for boundary demarcation, prevention 
of encroachments control of pests and diseases etc. shall be prepared by the 
States and implemented after they are approved by the Central Government. 
Central Government is closely monitoring the situation and is committed 
to provide all necessary assistance to the States and tackle this problem 
effectively.

1464. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that insecticides treated seeds have led to 
death of a large number of peacocks and other birds and animals; and 
(b) if so, whether the Ministry would control and regulate the manufacture and 
use of chemicals, fertilizers and ins ecticides in a manner as to prevent 
recurrence of such incidents?

AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The

peacocks due to consumption of pesticiude treated seeds in the agricultural 
fields, The list of peacocks that have been reported to have died because of 
consuming pesticide/ insecticide tr eated seed is enclosed Statement (See

(b) Government of India has enacted a comprehensive legislation called 
the "Insecticides Act, 1968" which infer alia regulates the manufacture, 
transport, distribution and use of pestic ides with a view to prevent risk to 
human beings, animals, birds and the en vironment. Moreover, the pesticides 
are registered under this comprehensive legislation after a detailed evaluation 
regarding their safety to the human beings, animals, birds and the 
environment. Pesticides, thus registered, if used as per the Good Agricultural 
Practice and prescribed manner, are no t likely to cause any death of any 
animals and birds including peacock.

Exorbitant price for TRICOX drug by M/s Themis 
1470. SHRI MUNAVVAR HASAN: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that M/s Themis had been selling TRICOX drug, 
meant for Tuberculosis, at exorbitant prices; and 
 if so, the details thereof and the action proposed to be taken against 
the Company? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and 
(b) Yes, Sir. As per the enquiry made by the Commissioner, Food and Drugs 
Administration, Gujarat, prima facie, M/s Themis Chemicals Limited had 
been selling TRICOX Tabs druing the period from 12.5.1992 to 3.8.1992 at 
a price higher than the price fixed by  the Government under Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1987 and the company has been issued a show cause notice 
in March, 2000 to that effect.

CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that M/s Tridoss is a sister concern of M/s 
WOCKHARDT MERIND and is availing exemption from Drug Price

 if so, the actio'.', proposed to be taken against the Company?

(b) M/s Tridoss has claimed exemption stating that it is a SSI Unit but it has 
not submitted price lists to Nationa l Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority

Fetilizer policy 
† 1472. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE: Will the Minister 
of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 the details for the new fertilizer policy formulated during current Five 
Year Plan; 
 whether there is any proposal to give new direction to the present 
fertilizer policy and to formulate its new structure, afresh; 
 if so, the details of the likely expenditure for this proposed objective; 
and 
 the policy adopted regarding the fertilizer policy for increasing the 
basic production capacity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (c) 
No new fertilizer policy has been formulated, so far, during the current Five 
Year Plan. However, the Government is in the process of formulating a long-
term fertilizer policy aiming at phased decontrol of fertilizer sector. The 
proposed long term policy will also dwell on issues such as joint ventures, 
creation   of   new   capacity,   WTO   related   matters,   removal   of 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
267 

RAJYA SABHA        [12 MARCH, 2001] 
distribution control on urea, balanced nutrient applications, eco-friendly 
fertilizer use etc. Besides, a new pricing policy for urea units based on the 
recommendations of the Expenditure Reforms Commission, for replacing the 
existing Retention Price-cum-Subsidy Scheme is under formulation of the 
Government. The likely expenditure for the proposed initiatives would 
depend on the outcome of parameters of Long Term Policy including New 
Pricing Policy for urea units, which are yet to be approved by the 
Government. 
(d) The Government policy has aimed at attaining the maximum possible 
degree of self-sufficiency in the production of nitrogenous fertilizers based on 
indigenous feed stocks. While the country is self-sufficient to the extent of 
about 90 per cent in the case of n itrogenous fertilizers, in the case of 
phosphates, the paucity of indigenous raw materials is a serious constraint in 
achieving the goal of self-sufficiency. The Government have, therefore, 
adopted a mixed strategy by going in for a combination of domestic 
production based on indigenous/imported rock phosphate and imported 
sulphur, domestic production based on imported intermediates like ammonia 
and phosphoric acid and import of the finished product, namely, DAP. 
Similary in the case of potash, there are no known commercially exploitable 
reserves in the country and the entire requirement of potassic fertilizers both 
for direct application as well as for manufacture of complex fertilizers is met 
through imports. 
Realising the constraints in the availability of gas, which is the preferred 
feedstock for nitrogenous fertilizers, and the near total dependence of the 
country on imported raw materials for production of phosphatic fertilizers, 
the Government have also been encouraging Indian companies to establish 
joint venture facilities with buy-back arrangements in other countries, which 
have rich reserves of natural gas and rock phosphate.

1478. MISS    MABEL    REBELLO:     Will    the    Minister    of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether UNFPA report has stated  that forests are now shrinking 
marginally, only in comparison to the period between 1950 and 1980, but 
dense forests are being lost and with galloping population, per person forest 
ratio is going down; and 
 if so, what corrective steps are being taken by Government to make 
the country green?

BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. But as per Stat e of Forest Report 1999, published by

km. and dense forests by 10098 sq. km. during the period 1996 to 1998. 
(b) Various measures taken to increase the foresvtree cover in the country 
are: 
(i) Afforestation     programmes     are     undertaken     by     State

assistance from Government of India. 
(ii) Externally Aided Projects are being implemented for the 
development and preservation of forests. 
(iii) Guidelines have been issued to all States'UTs to involve 
village communities in protection and regeneration of degraded 
forests.

Forest land for Sabarimala Temple 
1479. SHRI N-K. PREMACHANDRAN: 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether any proposal to allot forest land for development of Sabarimala 
Temple is pending with Government for decision; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 Government's reaction in the matter; 
 what are the reasons for the delay in allotting the required land to the 
Temple; and 
 by when the sanction is likely to be accorded in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (e) No, Sir. However, on earlier occasions, the Govemment of 
Kerala submitted ten proposals for diversion of forest land for creating different 
facilities in and around Ayyappa Temple at Sabarimala. Out of these seven 
proposals were approved. One proposal relating to diversion of 0.6 ha. of 
forest land for quarrying of rubble has been closed on 20.10.1998 for want of 
information from the State Government. The second proposal relating to 
construction of water treatment plant over 0.6 ha. forest land in Tiger Reserve 
was rejected on 15.12.2000, since it is not a permissible activity within a National 
Park/Sanctuary. 
The third proposal relates to diversion of 115.6 ha. of forest land for 
development of Rudravanam Complex around Lord Ayyappa Temple. While 
the proposal was being processed, the State Government came with another 
proposal for 20 ha. of forest land in the year 1995 for the same purpose. Out 
of the 20 ha. demanded by the State Government, 15 ha. falls in Tiger Reserve 
area and 5 ha. outside. According to section 29 of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972, only such activities can be allowed in the National Park/wildlife 
sanctuaries which are for betterment of wildlife. Thus the proposal for 
diversion  of 0.4225  hectare area  for construction of sewage 
286 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
treatment plant at Cheriyanavottam and 0.20 hectare for construction of a 
check-dam at Kunnar for water augmentation were approved on 26.11.98 and 
2.2.2000 respectively. Permissive use of 5.00 hectare at Pamba for parking 
facilities outside the Tiger Reserve was also allowed on 2.2.2000. 
A Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri O. Rajagopal and two 
Members of Parliament as members visited the area and gave certain 
recommendations about improvement and future development of facilities for 
pilgrims. According to this report, the pilgrim facilities are to be created 
outside the Tiger Reserve. On the recommendations of the Committee, the 
State Government has been requested on 8.6.2000 to initiate action on the 
recommendations and formulate a proposal accordingly for fresh 
consideration of the Ministry. In view of this the already submitted proposal 
for balance area has been closed. The Kerala Government has not submitted 
any fresh proposal as yet.

Black bucks in the country 
1482. SHRI ANANTA SETHI: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether the black buck population in the country has been 
diminishing; 
 if so, the reasons therefor; 
290 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
 the State-wise population of black bucks at present; and 
 the steps taken to protect the black buck from untimely death? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) No, Sir. 
 Does not arise. 
 State-wise population census of black buck has not been carried out. 
However, according to a research study conducted by Bombay 
Natural History Society, the estimated population of black  buck in 
the country in 1991  was between 29,000 to 
38,000. 
(d) The steps taken by the Government to protect the black buck 
are as follows; 
(i) Black buck has been included in the Schedule I of Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972, there by providing it highest degree of 
protection. Hunting of black buck has been prohibited. 
(ii) A network of 572 wildlife protected areas covering 4.6% of country's 
geographical area has been created for conservation of wild flora 
and fauna which has helped in protecting the habitat of black buck. 
(iii) Financial assistance is provided to the State Governments for 
development and management of protected areas. 
(iv) Raids are carried out by wildlife authorities to curb poaching and 
illegal trade of wild animals. 
(v) International trade in wildlife and its products has been regulated 
under the provisions of CITES (Convention on Internationa] Trade 
in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna). Export of all 
forms of wild animals including their parts and products is 
prohibited under the EXIM Policy. 
(vi) Regional and Sub-regional O ffices of Wildlife Preservation have 
been set up at the main export centres of the country to prevent 
smuggling of wildlife products.

Decline in Wildlife 
1488. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether the country's animal and bird life is shrinking; 
 if so, the reasons for the decline in the wildlife; and 
 the steps taken to prevent ecological doom in India? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) With the rising human population and increase in the 
pace of development, decline in the extent of wild habitat and reduction in 
wild animal population cannot be ruled out. 
(c) Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is being implemented to allow diversion 
of forest land for non-forestry purpose, only where it is absolutely necessary 
and to ensure that the quantum of diversion is bare minimum. Wherever 
permission of diversion of forest land for non-forestry purpose is granted, 
adequate safeguards are also provided for conservation of wildlife. 
Section 29 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 permits only such 
activities in National Parks/Wildlife Sanctuaries, which are for the betterment 
of wildlife. 
299 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
Hunting of all wild animals is banned under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972. Steps taken to prevent illegal hunting are as follows : 
(i) Setting up of Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee under 
the chairmanship of Secretary (Enviro nment and Forests) for control of 
poaching and illegal trade. Similar Committees have been established at the 
State and district level in various States. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation has been authorised to apprehend 
Offenders to launch prosecution in wildlife offences. 
(Hi) Assistance is provided to the State Governments for strengthening the 
protection measures through involvement of armed squads and strike forces 
drawn out of para-military forces and State Armed Constabulary. 
(iv) Strengthening the infrastructure under the Central Government and to 
ensure its presence in all sensitive areas.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. The Ministry of Environment 
and Forests have formulated National Forestry Action Programme (NFAP), a 
comprehensive strategic long term plan for the next twenty years to bring 
one third of the area of the country under

(b) The National Forestry Action Programme has five main 
components. They are: 
1. Protect Existing Forest Resources: It has three main-sub 
programmes: (i) forest protection, (ii) soil and water conservation, 
and (iii) protected areas and biodiversity conservation. 
 Improve Forest Productivity: It has four main sub-programmes (i) 
rehabilitation of degraded forests, (ii) research and technology development, 
(hi) development of Non Wood Forest Products and (iv) assisting private 
initiatives with community participation. 
 Reduce Total Demand: It has three main sub programmes for efficient

programmes (i) Central Forestry admi nistration, (ii) Central forestry

Problems of epileptic patients 
1496. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 whether, according to the report pu blished in the Indian Express, 
dated 14th November, 2000, over 10 millon epileptics in India suffer not so 
much due to lack of access to drugs or treatment, but of social stigma and 
availability of poor quality drugs; if so, whether Government are aware of 
the problems faced by the epileptics; 
 if so, the steps taken by Government on the above report; and 
 if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Epilepsy is a brain 
disorder occurring due to excess elect rical discharge em anating from the 
neurons of the brain. 
The control of epilepsy depends upon correct diagnosis, adequate dosage 
of anti-epileptic drugs, and compliance by the patients. Epilepsy is also 
associated with misconception and myths about its nature and, therefore, 
some people with epilepsy do not seek medical treatment, which is not only 
affordable but can also be very effective in the control of epilepsy. 
The Indian Epilepsy Association, th e Indian Academy of Neurology and 
Neurological Society of India disse minate information about epilepsy 
amongst doctors, other professional and the public. The National Institute 
of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences, Bangalore, has developed a district 
model of epilepsy care to provide training to district medical officers to 
diagnose and treat people with epilepsy. They are also trained to provide 
counselling to the patients and their families to remove the stigma attached 
to epilepsy. 
As far as the quality of drugs under CGHS is concerned, the CGHS 
procures all the listed formulary drugs from the MSO, which tests each lot 
of medicine batch-wise, and supplies are effected only 
ins 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
after the receipt of satisfactory test report from the Government laboratory. 
The medicines are supplied to CGHS  beneficiaries on advice of the 
attending physician.

1529. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RES OURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased

(a) the action taken/proposed to be taken to make registration of marriages 
compulsory throughout the country  to eliminate child marriage and

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
342 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the stringent punishment proposed for parents involved in marriage of 
minor children for early elimination of child marriage from the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA M AH A J AN): (a) 
Registration of marriages solemnised or contracted under the Indian Christian 
Marriage Act, 1872, the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936 and the 
Special Marriage Act, 1954 is compul sory. Section 8 of the Hindu Marriage 
Act, 1955 provides that if the State Government is of opinion that it is 
necessary or expedient so to do, it may provide that the entering of the 
particulars of Hindu marriages in the Hindu marriage register shall be 
compulsory in the State or in any part thereof, whether in all cases or in such 
cases as may be specified. Certain State Governments, namely, the States of 
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Himachal Prad esh and Karnataka have State Acts 
providing for compulsory registration of marriages in those States. 
Registration of marriages solemnised otherwise than under the Special 
Marriage Act, 1954 is permissible under section 16 of the said Act if such 
marriage fulfil certain conditions as laid down under chapter III of that Act. 
The question of making registration of Hindu marriages compulsory could 
thus be considered by the State Governments as per the local situations 
prevailing in those States. 
(b) The National Commission for Women (NCW) had proposed 
amendments in the Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929, suggesting, inter 
alia, enhancement of punishment for the parent/guardian/or any other person 
having the charge of the minor when the minor contracts child marriage. The 
proposal made by NCW has been forwarded to the Ministry of Law, Justice 
& Company Affairs (Legislative Department) which has taken up the matter 
with the State Governments.

Inclusion of Human Rights and Duties in School Curriculum 
1537. PROF. RAM DEO BHANDARY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether Justice Varma Committee has recommended to make Human 
Rights and Duties a compulsory subject for teaching in schools and at other 
higher education levels; 
 if so, the details of other recommendations made in this regard; and 
 the progress made in implementation of these recommendations, so 
far? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) The Justice Varma Committee has 
recommended that there is  need for a fundamental transformation in the 
direction and approach to curricula for teaching Fundamental Duties in 
schools and TEACHER EDUCATION institutions. The Committee has also 
made recommendations for incorporating Fundamental Duties in the 
courses^»rogrammes for higher and professional education. 
 The other recommendations of the Committee include generating 
awareness and consciousness of Fund amental Duties, optimizing benefits 
from the existing schemes4>rogrammes, protection and improvement of 
environment, elimination of gender bias, reorie nting teacher education 
programmes, ensuring the responsibilities of people's representatives from 
Panchayats to Parliament, obligation of Public Administration and Civil 
Servants, administration of Justice, role of business, industry and media in 
creating awareness of the need to appr eciate and internalize the concept and 
practice of Fundamental Duties. 
 The Report has been circulated to concerned Ministries of the Central 
Government and all State Governments for follow-up action. 
353 

RAJYA SABHA [12 MARCH, 2001] 
Most of the Ministries have accepte d the recommendations and have started 
implementation also. The progress made in implementation of these 
recommendations is as follows: 
 Preamble and Article 51A of the Constitution is being printed in 
NCERT publications. 
 The New Curricular Framework brought out by the NCERT highlights 
the need for teaching Human Rights and Duties to students at all levels. 
 UGC has decided that Human Rights Education Scheme of University 
Grants Commission be renamed as "Human Rights and Duties 
Education." 
 Curriculum Development Committee has been constituted by UGC to 
prepare model curriculum in various courses in Human Rights and 
Duties Education. 
 UGC has identified Seventeen Universities for inclusion of Post-
Graduate Degree/DiplomaCertificate Courses on Human Rights and 
Duties Education. 
 Modules of Fundamental Rights and National Values have been made 
available to Teacher Education Institutions. 
 The Police Division of the Ministry of Home Affairs has requested the 
Director, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy, 
Hyderabad to devise a module on the lines suggested by the High 
Level Committee where senior IPS officer can be sent for re-furbishing 
their attitudes and aptitudes in this regard. 
 A National Judicial Academy has been set up under the Ministry of 
Home Affairs to inter-alia provide in-service training to Judicial 
Officers, to provide continuing e ducation to Judici al Officers of 
StatesAJnion Territories, to pr omote the highest standards of 
professional competence and pr actice and to study the court 
Management and Administration of Justice from all over India. 
 The Ministry of Commerce and Industry has sent the report to 
354 

[12 MARCH, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
the  Apex  Chambers of Commerce  and  Industry  for wider 
dissemination amongst their members. 
 The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has shown its willingness 
for full cooperation in disseminating messages on Fundamental Duties to 
the citizens of the country. In this regard all the Stations of All India 
Radio and Doordarshan have been issued instructions to arrange 
appropriate programmes on the subj ect to generate awareness among 
masses. DAVP has undertaken the steps to transmit message on 
Fundamental Duties to the citizens of the country by releasing Press 
advertisement in English, Hindi and language papers, DAVP has also 
brought out a small folder containing duties of citizens towards the 
country. This folder will be primarily distributed in schools and 
colleges. 
 The Government of India has issued instructions to all Central 
Government Ministries/Departments as well as to State Governments 
to issue Citizen Charters for all organizations with a large public 
interface. The Citizen Charters are in the nature of commitments made 
by Government organizations to respond to the needs of the citizens 
and to deliver services according to prescribed standards.

1538. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether the system of re-appointing Professors after 62 years of age is 
being currently applied in few Central Universities only and not in all of 
them; 
 if so, the reasons therefor; 
 whether it would be extended to all other Central Universities 
also; and 
(d) what is the general feeling about this system? 
355

MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) According to the UGC Notification 
on revision of pay scales, minimum qualification for appointment of teachers 
in universities and colleges and other measures for maintenance of standards, 
1998, the age of superannuation of univ ersity and college teachers would be 
62 years and thereafter no extension in service should be given. However, it 
will be open to a university or college to re-employ a superannuated teacher

cases of parents and relatives;

Act, 1956 as amended in 1978 and in 1986. 
(u) Economic package of Rs. 10,000''- in fixed deposit with monthly interest

in some eco-systems of the countr y. Under the National Bioresource 
Development Board projects in animals, microbial and plant diversity have 
been taken up.

sequencing project would have been very high. It was also known that the 
information would be available in public domain, accordingly Indian genome 
initiative programme was started. Recently programmes have been 
formulated to utilize this large information base, specially in the areas of 
functional and application genomics, micro array technology, sequencing of 
microbes, pharmacogenomics etc. This is a continuing exercise. The results 
from these projects are likely to be available during next 2-5 years.

SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, I move: 
"That this House disapproves the Taxation Laws 
(Amendment) Ordinance, 2001 (N0.2 of 2001) promulgated by 
the President on the 3,d February, 2001." 
Sir, Parliament has been convened by the President and after 
that, the Ordinance was promulgated. We are all for providing help to 
the Gujarat Government and people on all aspects. The nation has 
responded very well and contributions and help is pouring in and the 
international community has also responded very well. Promulgating 
an Ordinance, enhancing the income-tax by a surcharge is not at all 
advisable in this context. There are so many other means for the 
Government to mobilise resources. Before putting a surcharge on the 
common people, the Government should have been honest to get the 
money from the corporate houses. There are tax 
448

arrears and NPAs to the tune of  Rs.62,ooo crores, due from big 
businesses, big industrialists. Even if we calculate a small interest, it 
becomes more than Rs. 1,00,000 crores. The Government has, many 
times, promised that steps will be taken to get the dues. Once the hon. 
Finance Minister said that if necessary, we would pass a legislation for 
that purpose. But nothing has been done. Still a huge amount of tax is 
pending. If the Government is willing to mobilise resources, why has 
nothing been done to get this amount from the corporate sector, big 
businesses and big industrialists? If even one-third of the amount is 
realised, we get at least Rs.30,000 crores. Nothing has been done for 
that. Always the burden is passed on to the common people. We have 
seen in the Budget also that so  many benefits are given to the 
corporate sector. The surcharge on income-tax and the surcharge on 
corporate tax, have been reduced. 10 per cent surcharge on income 
tax, 10 per cent surcharge on corporate tax has been removed. But 2 
per cent surcharge on income tax still remains on the common people, 
on the employees and on the taxpayers. Sir, an Ordinance on 
surchage is improper. The Government should not promulgate an 
Ordinance for income tax surcharges. So, the Government has no 
consideration for the Parliament's right. After convening both Houses 
of Parliament, how can the Government promulgate an Ordinance? It 
is an extraordinary step. In the past also, the Government has 
promulgated such Ordinances and there were discussions here and 
the Government stands committed on that. After convening the 
Parliament, promulgating Ordinances is a challenge to the functioning 
of the Parliamentary Democracy. Sir,  if the Government is willing to 
mobilise resources for helping the Gujarat people and the State 
Government of Gujarat, they have to resort to some other methods. 
There are ample sources and methods to get resources for the 
Gujarat people and the Government. So, I appeal to the House that 
this Ordinance, promulgated after convening the Parliament, should 
be rejected. Thank you, Sir.

the High Court were refixed. As a result of that refixation, certain 
anomalies came into existence. And, one of the result of the 
anomalies was that the staff of the High Court, in a large number of 
categories, were getting much more than what the people in 
equivalent categories in other Government services were getting. The 
disparities were quite large. T herefore, a Group of  Ministers was 
appointed in the early 90's to go into this question. The Group of 
Ministers suggested this legislatio n, because, under the provisions of 
Article 229 (2), the salaries can norm ally be fixed by the Chief Justice, 
unless there is a legislation which provides for them. So, a legislation 
was suggested. In 1994, this legislation was introduced in the House. 
It was referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee. The 
Standing Committee went into the whole question, had a detailed 
hearing and approved the legislation,  which I commend for the 
acceptance of this hon.  House. 
I may just give in brief, the spirit of this legislation. It provides 
details about the salaries which the staff of the High Court would be 
entitled to in each grade, because, by virtue of the judicial 
pronouncements, their grades had been increased. Therefore, there is 
a protection scheme also for thos e whose pay-scales have been 
increased. The protection scheme is provided in Section 3 that if a 
court servant is already getting something which is higher than what 
he is entitled to, under the Schedule, he will continue to get that salary 
till he reaches that particular point of his grade so that there is no 
material effect of actually the salaries coming down, excepting that his 
pay  will get frozen at the highest point and he   will not
